name: Clobetasol skin-lightening creams

card.summary: Illicit whitening creams that contain the super-potent steroid clobetasol propionate, used by people seeking a lighter or more even complexion.
card.aka: Steroid-laced whitening creams; adulterated lightening creams
card.note: Clobetasol is prescription-only in the US and not approved for skin lightening; documented harms include skin thinning and adrenal suppression.

quick.overview:
Clobetasol propionate is a super-high-potency topical corticosteroid prescribed for conditions such as eczema, psoriasis and lichen sclerosus. Some skin-lightening creams sold outside regulated channels contain it, often undeclared.

The appearance goal is a lighter-looking, more even complexion. Steroid creams can thin and lighten skin, but regulators and dermatologists document serious harms, and the FDA has not approved it for lightening.
quick.how: In reality these products are sold as cosmetic whitening creams in some beauty stores and online, sometimes without ingredient labels. Prescribed clobetasol, by contrast, is used short-term under medical supervision for inflammatory skin disease.
quick.risks: Reported harms of misuse include skin thinning, bruising, acne, stretch marks, high blood pressure and high blood sugar; serious risks include adrenal suppression and Cushing's syndrome. In the US it is prescription-only, and non-prescription sales are illegal.

lead: Clobetasol propionate is a potent topical corticosteroid in the top 'super-high potency' class of the US seven-group system, used medically for eczema, dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus and other conditions [1]. It has also been found in skin-lightening creams that are sold without a prescription [1][2].

People who use such creams are generally after a lighter or more even skin tone. Skin-whitening products as a category are used widely, with surveys cited by Wikipedia reporting about 77 percent of Nigerian women, 52 percent of Senegalese women and 25 percent of Malian women using lightening products in 2013 [2].

Wikipedia notes that the FDA has not approved clobetasol for skin whitening and that such creams turn up in New York City beauty stores and online, sometimes at concentrations above what prescription products allow [1].

angle.text: Users apply the cream hoping for a lighter complexion. Clinicians document harms from this use, and the lightening is a side effect of a steroid rather than an approved purpose.

paras: Medically, clobetasol propionate treats eczema, contact and seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus and alopecia areata, among others [1]. Cosmetic use for lightening is described as controversial and unapproved [1].

Common effects include irritation, dryness, redness, pimples and telangiectasia; serious risks include cellulitis, adrenal suppression and Cushing's syndrome [1]. For lightening misuse, reported harms include skin thinning, bruising, acne, stretch marks, hypertension and high blood glucose [1].

Wikipedia's skin-whitening article describes long-term use of topical steroids over large areas as able to cause systemic effects, including skin thinning, glaucoma, cataracts and osteoporosis, and lists clobetasol with mercury and hydroquinone as problem ingredients in whiteners [2].
Enforcement is described as inconsistent across countries; in the UK many whiteners are illegal but still sold [2]. Clobetasol propionate was patented in 1968 and entered medical use in 1978 [1].
No studies found on clobetasol as a lightening agent in controlled trials; the available literature is on its medical use and on adverse events from misuse [1][2].
